newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian monsoon rains progress but skip pockets.
newsitem.headline: Indian monsoon rains progress but skip pockets.

text.p: Southwest monsoon rains in India has progressed well but sparse rains in pockets in two large states could affect crop prospects in the region, officials and crop analysts said on Wednesday.
"The overall progress of the monsoon is very good," said S. R. Khalsi, a senior official of the Indian Meteorological Department.

Khalsi said the central state of Madhya Pradesh and eastern Orissa had received good rains this week. But rains in Vidarbha and Marathwada regions in western Maharashtra state and Telengana and Coastal areas in southern Andhra Pradesh were deficient, he said.
Analysts said lack of rains could hit rice and groundnut crops in Andhra Pradesh and soybean and pulses output in Maharashtra.

The government in a mid-season review of the June-September monsoon said on Monday that India was poised for the 10th successive normal monsoon with 29 of the 35 meteorological sub-divisions in the country receiving normal to excess rainfall.
"This year the adverse impact of El-Nino, if any, is not yet visible and monsoon circulation pattern is quite well established and healthy," the government statement said.
El Nino warm water currents raisesthe water temperature off the coast of South America and can disrupt weather patterns worldwide, creating drought in some areas and floods in others.
The statement said scientific analysis of data over the past one hundred years shows that there is no one-to-one correspondence between El Nino and the Indian monsoon rainfall.
The south-west monsoon advanced into southern Kerala state on June 9, a week late than the normal onset of the monsoon.
The statement said the onset of the monsoon over other parts of the country was also delayed by about a week.

"One of the problems of the weather office is they are looking at the amount of the rainfall and not at distribution," said S. M. Virmani, an official with the Hyderabad-based International Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics.
Virmani said the timing of sowing operations was very crucial. "One day's delay means one percent loss in yield," said Virmani.
He said sowing of soybean, groundnut and rice in Andhra Pradesh had been delayed by three weeks and would lead to rescheduling of the second crop.
"Overall the monsoon is quite encouraging, it was rather scary a fortnight ago," said one commodity analyst who asked not to be identified.
"We are hopeful it will be the 10th good monsoon." Khalsi said.
